title: Workflows versus agents
objective: Know the common workflow patterns, when a fixed workflow beats an agent, and when an agent is worth its cost.

sources.title: Anthropic: Building effective agents: workflows ("orchestrated through predefined code paths") versus agents; prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer; "finding the simplest solution possible"

simplifies: Real systems mix these patterns. The diagram shows routing; the other patterns are described in the captions.

steps.caption: Two kinds of system. Workflows: model calls and tools "orchestrated through predefined code paths". Agents: the model directs its own process and tool use.
Prompt chaining: a fixed sequence, where each call works on the previous one's output. Code checks in between (a "gate") keep it on track.
Routing: classify the input, then send it to a specialised follow-up. A billing question and a tech question each get the prompt built for them.

predict.prompt: A billing question and a technical question arrive. With routing, what happens?

options.text: Both go to one general prompt
Each is classified, then handled by the prompt made for its kind
options.explanation: Right. Specialised prompts do better than one prompt trying to do everything.

options.text: An agent decides everything from scratch each time
options.explanation: Routing is a fixed step: classify, then send on.

steps.caption: Parallelization: split a task into independent parts that run at the same time (sectioning), or run the same task several times and compare (voting).

Orchestrator-workers: a central model breaks the task down, hands parts to workers, and combines the results. Unlike parallelization, the parts aren't fixed in advance; the orchestrator decides them for each input.
Evaluator-optimizer: one call writes, another evaluates and gives feedback, in a loop, for example a translation polished over a few rounds.
Agents suit open-ended problems where you can't predict the steps. The price: higher costs, and errors that can compound.

predict.prompt: Password resets follow the same three steps every time. Workflow or agent?

options.text: A workflow: the steps are known, so fixed code is cheaper and more predictable
options.explanation: Right. An agent's freedom buys nothing here and adds cost and risk.
Freedom to choose steps only helps when the steps aren't known in advance.
A workflow can call the reset tool at the right step.

steps.caption: The guide's advice: find the simplest solution possible, and add complexity only when it's needed.

critique.prompt: A proposal: an autonomous agent with 15 tools handles password resets (always the same 3 steps). It has no step limit, and nobody measures whether its answers are right.

risks.text: An agent for a fixed three-step task adds cost and unpredictability for nothing
risks.why: A short workflow does the same steps every time, cheaper and easier to test.

risks.text: 15 tools for a password reset gives it far more power than the job needs
risks.why: Offer only the tools a task needs (OWASP calls the opposite "excessive agency").

risks.text: With no step limit, a confused run can loop and burn money
risks.why: Add a stopping condition such as a maximum number of steps.

risks.text: Nobody measures whether its answers are right
risks.why: Without evaluation, you won't notice when it gets worse.

risks.text: It uses a model at all
risks.why: Models are fine here, for example to understand the request; the problem is the open-ended agent.

risks.text: Users type their request in their own words
risks.why: That's the point of a language model in front.

critique.hint: Ask what the task needs: how many steps, which tools, and how you'd know it works.

options.explanation: Useful, but it treats a symptom of using an agent where none is needed.

options.text: Replace the agent with a fixed three-step workflow
options.explanation: Right. It removes the open-ended loop, most of the tools and most of the risk in one move.
Better, but the task still doesn't need an agent.

critique.explain: Match the system to the task: known steps call for a workflow. Then give it only the tools it needs, and measure whether it works.

quiz.prompt: What's the difference between orchestrator-workers and parallelization?

options.text: Orchestrator-workers runs one step at a time
options.explanation: Workers can run in parallel too; the difference is who decides the subtasks.
They differ in whether the split is fixed or decided per input.

options.text: In orchestrator-workers, the subtasks aren't fixed in advance: the orchestrator decides them per input
options.explanation: Right. Parallelization splits work in a way decided ahead of time.

quiz.prompt: When is an agent worth its extra cost?

options.explanation: Many model tasks are best as a single call or a workflow.

options.text: For open-ended problems where you can't predict the steps
options.explanation: Right. Otherwise a workflow is simpler and cheaper.

options.text: When the task has exactly three steps
